explanations.explanation: Cousins it is. Abigail, Amasa's mother, and Zeruiah, Joab's mother, are sisters, so their sons are cousins. Joab is one of David's commanders, and he's the man Absalom replaced with Amasa. That family reunion is going to need a seating chart.

The mothers settle this one. Amasa's mother is Abigail, and Joab's mother is Zeruiah (2 Samuel 17:25). Those are two different women, so these two aren't brothers. They're sisters, which makes their sons cousins. Joab's actual brother is Abishai, who shows up in the next chapter as Zeruiah's son.
These two aren't strangers at all. Abigail, Amasa's mother, is the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. Strangers don't have mothers who are sisters. That makes Amasa and Joab cousins.

explanations.answer: The people are hungry and tired and thirsty
explanations.explanation: That's the reason they give: “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” So out comes the full spread: beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep and cheese. That's a lot of cargo for three men, friend.

explanations.answer: The king sent word asking for supplies
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say David sent word. The three men come to meet him, and they give their own reason: “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” Nobody's asked, and they bring it anyway. I think that makes it feel even more like a gift.

explanations.answer: They want a place in the king's army
explanations.explanation: No army spot is asked for here. What they say is, “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” The reason is all about David's people. And they back it up with beds, wheat, honey and sheep.

explanations.answer: He will march out with them
explanations.explanation: David tells his troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” He says it right after splitting them under three commanders: Joab, Abishai and Ittai. So the king says he'll go in with them. Hold that thought, because his people have something to say about it.

explanations.answer: He will wait for more men
explanations.explanation: There's no waiting for reinforcements in these verses. David reviews his troops, splits them into three, and says, “I will surely march out with you as well.” That's a king saying he'll be right there with them.

explanations.answer: He will talk to Absalom first
explanations.explanation: Talking to Absalom first isn't in the plan. David's words about his son come a few verses later, when he commands the commanders to treat Absalom gently. Here he tells his troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” So the king is headed to the field, at least for now.

explanations.answer: He is worth ten thousand of them
explanations.explanation: They tell him, “But you are worth ten thousand of us.” They say that if they have to flee, or even if half of them die, the enemy will not care about them. David is the one the people value. So they ask him to support them from the city. Ten thousand to one is a number nobody can argue with.

explanations.answer: Absalom's army is far too big
explanations.explanation: The people never say Absalom's army is too big. Their words are, “But you are worth ten thousand of us.” It's all about how much David is worth to them. I'd say the whole speech is one big compliment.

explanations.answer: He has never led them in battle
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about David never leading them in battle. His people simply say, “But you are worth ten thousand of us.” That's about his worth, not his record. It's a pretty big compliment to give a boss.

True. David answers, “I will do whatever seems best to you.” Then he stands beside the gate while the troops march out by hundreds and by thousands. A boss who takes advice from the team? That's rare, friend.

The text says the opposite. David tells his people, “I will do whatever seems best to you,” and he stands beside the gate while all the troops march out. So he does stay back from the battle. He started with “I will surely march out with you,” and then he listened.

Gently is the word: “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” That's David's one order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai about his son. I think a father's heart is in that sentence. And he says it's for his sake.
Firmly isn't in the order. David says, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” Gently and firmly are pretty different words. I think a father's heart is in that sentence.
Close in sound, but the word is gently. David commands, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” And he says it's for his sake.

It wasn't only the three. The text says, “…all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom.” Joab, Abishai and Ittai heard it, and so did everybody else. Keep that in your pocket, baker, because it comes back soon.

Right, the whole crowd heard it. The text says, “…all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom.” Joab, Abishai and Ittai weren't the only ones. Remember that when a soldier says, “…we heard the king command you…” a little later.
The forest of Ephraim, friend. That's where David's army marches to engage Israel. Keep an eye on those trees, because they matter in this story. When you're in a forest, always look up.

The Valley of Elah belongs to a different story: Saul and the men of Israel camped there against the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2). This battle takes place in the forest of Ephraim. Different battle, different spot.
The text never sends this battle to Moab. It says the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. Trees, not plains. And a few verses later, the forest turns out to take more lives than the sword.

True. The people of Israel, Absalom's side, are defeated by David's servants in the forest of Ephraim. The text says the slaughter is great that day, twenty thousand men. I think this is a heavy part of the story. Take a breath, baker.
The text says the opposite. The people of Israel are defeated by David's servants. The slaughter is great that day, twenty thousand men. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

Head. Absalom is riding his mule when it goes under the thick branches of a large oak, and his head is caught fast in the tree. The mule keeps going, so he is suspended in midair. That's the whole reason one of David's men has something to report.
Not his foot. The text says his head is caught fast in the tree. The mule goes under the thick branches of a large oak and keeps going, leaving Absalom suspended in midair.
No cloak in this verse. The text says his head is caught fast in the tree as the mule goes under the thick branches. The mule keeps going, and Absalom is left suspended in midair.

explanations.answer: He asks why the man didn't strike him
explanations.explanation: Joab answers with a question. First he says, “You just saw him!” Then he asks why the man didn't strike Absalom to the ground right there. He adds that he would have given the man ten shekels of silver and a warrior's belt.

explanations.answer: He tells the man to go tell the king
explanations.explanation: Joab never says to tell the king. He starts with, “You just saw him!” Then he asks why the man didn't strike Absalom to the ground. Going to the king isn't anywhere in his answer.

explanations.answer: He orders the man to cut him down
explanations.explanation: Joab doesn't give an order to cut Absalom down. He says, “You just saw him!” and asks why the man didn't strike Absalom to the ground right there. Then he brings up ten shekels of silver and a warrior's belt. It's questions first, rewards second.

Joab's half is right: ten shekels of silver and a warrior's belt. But the man says, “Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the son of the king.” So he says no at a thousand. That's a hundred times the silver Joab offered, and the answer is still no.

The man says no, even at a thousand. His words: “Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the son of the king.” Joab offered ten shekels and a belt. A hundred times the silver, same answer, friend.

The man says the opposite. He tells Joab that if he had jeopardized his own life, “you would have abandoned me.” So he doesn't think Joab would have stood by him. That's why he wouldn't touch Absalom, even for a thousand shekels.
That's right. He says that if he had jeopardized his own life, “you would have abandoned me.” So no, he doesn't think Joab would have stood by him. I think he's seen how these things go.
After the ram's horn, “…the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them.” So the chasing stops. The text says Joab is the one who held them back.
It's the opposite. After Joab blows the ram's horn, “…the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them.” They don't go deeper. They stop.

explanations.answer: March back to the king's gate
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they march back to the gate. It says, “…the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them.” They stop chasing. Where they go next isn't in these verses.

explanations.answer: Throw him in a pit under stones
explanations.explanation: They take Absalom, cast him into a large pit in the forest, and pile a huge mound of stones over him. I think this is a quiet, sad ending to a loud life. It's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Carry him back to King David
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they carry him to David. It says they cast him into a large pit in the forest and pile a huge mound of stones over him. That's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Bury him in his father's tomb
explanations.explanation: There's no tomb here. The text says they cast Absalom into a large pit in the forest and pile a huge mound of stones over him. This is a heavy part, and I think it feels heavier because it's so plain.

explanations.answer: Flee each to his own home
explanations.explanation: All the Israelites fled, each to his home. The people who followed Absalom scatter and head back where they came from. Nobody's marching together anymore.
Amasa is the man Absalom put over the army (2 Samuel 17:25), but the text never says anyone makes him king. It says all the Israelites fled, each to his home. Nobody's planning a coronation.

explanations.answer: Surrender to David at the gate
explanations.explanation: There's no surrender at the gate in these verses. The text says all the Israelites fled, each to his home. David is standing beside the gate, but they head home instead.
Son. Absalom said, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name.” So he gave the pillar his name, and to this day it's called Absalom's Monument. I think that's a lonely thing to say.
The word he uses is son. Absalom said, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name.” So he set up the pillar in the King's Valley and gave it his own name.

Brother isn't what he says. His words are, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name.” He gave the pillar his own name, and it's called Absalom's Monument. I think that's a sad little reason to build a pillar.
